title: Build the Minimum-Cost Infrastructure Network
real_world_story: The city has a list of all possible roads and utility connections it could build, each with a construction cost. It must choose a subset of these connections that links every facility while spending as little as possible overall.

real_world_connection.input_represents: All candidate roads and utility lines and their construction costs
real_world_connection.output_represents: The minimum total cost to connect every facility
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Building a minimum spanning network (spanning tree)

problem_statement: Given N facilities numbered 0 to N-1 and E candidate undirected connections with costs, find the minimum total cost required to connect all N facilities into a single connected network.
task: Return the total cost of the minimum-cost spanning network. If the graph cannot connect all facilities, return -1.
input_format: The first line contains two integers N and E. The next E lines each contain three integers u v w describing a candidate connection between facilities u and v with construction cost w.
output_format: Print the minimum total construction cost that connects all facilities, or -1 if they cannot all be connected.

examples.explanation: The cheapest way to connect all facilities uses the connections 2-3 (4), 0-3 (5) and 0-1 (10), for a total of 19.

expected_algorithm.name: Kruskal's Algorithm
expected_algorithm.reason: Sorting candidate connections by cost and adding the cheapest connection that does not create a cycle yields the minimum-cost spanning tree.

hint: Sort all candidate connections by construction cost.
Add each candidate in order if it connects two still-unconnected groups.
Use a union-find structure to track which facilities are already connected.
Stop once N - 1 connections have been selected.
real_world_takeaway: Kruskal's algorithm lets a city build a fully connected infrastructure network at the minimum construction cost by choosing the cheapest non-redundant connections.
